title: Contemporary trends in software development
everyday: How programs are built, and what the tools do for the programmer.
weight: About 7 marks of 120 in the exam.

screens.title: Procedural programming: breaking a program into smaller jobs
screens.goal: Describe procedural programming and say what a procedure is.

note.title: Programming paradigms
lines: A programming paradigm is an approach to organising and writing a program.
You study two paradigms in this unit: procedural programming and object-oriented programming.
This screen is about procedural programming. Screens 2 to 6 are about object-oriented programming, and screen 7 compares the two.

say: A [[procedure|1]] is a named, self-contained block of code that carries out one task.
You write it once. The program calls it by name whenever that task is needed.
Procedural programmers plan from the top down. First they name the whole task: make lasagne.
Then they split it into smaller jobs: meat sauce, cheese sauce, assemble, bake.
Then they write the steps inside each job. Each job becomes a named procedure.
Splitting the whole task into jobs, then into steps, is called top-down design.
Inside each procedure the computer carries out the steps in order, one after another.
Top-down design is how you plan the program. Step by step is how each procedure runs.

note.title: Three names you will meet
lines: Named blocks of instructions are called procedures, functions or methods. The name depends on the language and the book.
The exam mark schemes use all three names.
These lessons treat them as the same idea. In C#, the language you use, they are called methods.

picture.title: A main recipe card that calls smaller cards
lines: The main card is where cooking starts. It does not hold every step itself.
It says: make the meat sauce, make the cheese sauce, assemble, bake. Each of those has its own card.
In a program, Main is where the program starts, like the main recipe card. Each smaller card is a procedure that Main calls.
match: Breaking lasagne into sauces, assembly and baking
One small card, such as make the meat sauce
The title on a small card
Now make the meat sauce, written on the main card
The main card, where cooking starts
breaks: A cook can improvise. A computer follows its programmed instructions exactly. That includes when to call a procedure and what to do when it returns.
A recipe card is read by a person. The computer carries out a procedure. It repeats steps or calls other procedures only when the code says so.

anim.title: Watch the data move through Main and CalculateSum
anim.lead: CalculateSum is a small procedure. Press Next to follow one step at a time and watch where each value goes.
steps: The program starts in Main. Nothing is stored yet. The boxes on the right are the variables this program will use.
Line 3 runs. The data value 4 is stored in a variable named num1. num1 is the name of the box. 4 is the data inside it.
Line 4 runs. The data value 7 is stored in the variable num2.
Line 5 calls CalculateSum by name. Main pauses here and hands over two values.
The value 4 from num1 is copied into the parameter a. The value 7 from num2 is copied into the parameter b. The parameters get copies. num1 and num2 keep their own values.
Line 10 processes the data: a + b is 4 + 7, which makes 11.
The result 11 is returned to Main and stored in the variable sum. 11 is new data produced by the processing.
Line 6 outputs the data in sum. The screen shows: The sum is 11.

Finished. num1, num2 and sum are variables: named places that hold data. 4, 7 and 11 are the data values. Adding is the processing. CalculateSum is a method in this C# program. It is the named procedure from the recipe card, called by name to do one job.

parts.head: Procedural programming: the textbook definition
parts.say: An approach to developing a solution. The program operates on data and is organised in self-contained blocks called 'procedures'. The logic of the program is actioned by calling the procedures.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19) and the class presentation. The specification does not define it.

parts.head: What the examiner has credited
points: 2024 Q5(a) gave one mark each for PROCEDURAL, STEP BY STEP and SEQUENTIAL: in procedural programming a programmer specifies step by step what a program must do, and instructions are carried out in a sequential manner.

The 2025 Q7 mark scheme lists these procedural features. Use of procedures, functions or subroutines. Step-by-step instructions. Top-down design. Use of functions to solve problems. An example of a procedural language, such as C.
parts.src: the 2024 Q5(a) and 2025 Q7 mark schemes

parts.head: Say it in your own words
parts.say: A procedure is a named, self-contained block of code that carries out a task and can be called when needed. Procedural programs are planned top-down and each procedure runs step by step.

try.stem: Which of these best describes a procedure?

opts: A named, self-contained block of code that carries out a task when it is called
A list of every variable a program uses
The file where the finished program is stored
A drawing of the whole program

try.why: A procedure is written once, given a name, and called whenever that job is needed.

screens.title: Object-oriented programming: keeping data and methods together
screens.goal: Describe object-oriented programming and say what an object is.

say: Every program stores data and has procedures, functions or methods that work on it.
[[Data|1]] is stored information with a value, such as a game character's position, 0.
A method is a named block of instructions that performs a task. It is like the procedures on screen 1.
In procedural programming you organise the program around its procedures.
In [[object-oriented programming|2]] you organise it around objects.
An object groups a piece of related data with the methods that work on that data.
Object-oriented programs still use named procedures, methods or functions. They are kept beside the data they belong to.

anim.title: Meet Alex: one object, one piece of data, one method
anim.lead: Alex is a character in a game. Press Next to see what the program stores and what happens when a method runs.
steps: This is Alex, a character in a game. Alex is standing on square 0.
The program stores Alex's position as data: position = 0. The stored value tells the program where to draw Alex.
Alex also has a method called Move. A method is a named block of instructions that performs a task. Here are its three instructions.
The program calls Move. First instruction: read the stored position. It is 0.
Second instruction: add 1 to it. 0 + 1 makes 1.
Third instruction: store the new value. position is now 1.
The program draws Alex at the stored position, so Alex now appears on square 1. Changing the data changed what you see.
Labels: position is data. Move is a method. The object is the grouping of Alex's data and methods in one place.
One more thing. This card is a picture of the object. In the running program the object is a block of memory holding position. Move's code can read and change it.

picture.title: The same character as the program sees it
lines: One object, alex. Its data: position. Its method: Move.
A second character would be a second object with its own position.
Main gets objects to do things: alex.Move() asks the alex object to run its Move method.
match: Alex's position and Move kept together
breaks: Alex looks like a person. A program object is data and methods stored together. It has no body and makes no decisions of its own.
Here Alex's data is changed only by Alex's own Move method. Real programs can also let objects pass data to each other when the programmer chooses.

parts.head: First, a word you need: property
parts.say: An object's characteristics are called properties. Alex's Position is a property: a named characteristic with a current value, 0. Move is not a property. It is a method, something the object can do.

parts.head: Object-oriented programming: the textbook definition
parts.say: An approach to developing a solution where the focus is on data rather than processes. The data and the methods that operate on the data are contained within a single object class. The methods are the program code.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19) and the class presentation. The specification does not define it.
points: A class is the plan an object is made from. Screen 3 explains it. For now: Alex's data and Move are kept together in one place.

parts.head: Object: the textbook definition
parts.say: A self-contained element that contains the properties and methods needed to access and manipulate data values.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19) and the class presentation. The specification does not define it.
points: access means read the value, as Move reads position
manipulate means change the value, as Move stores 1
self-contained means the data and methods are grouped in the one object
data values means the stored position

parts.head: What the examiner has credited
points: 2024 Q5(a) gave one mark each for OBJECT ORIENTED, OBJECTS and DATA. A full answer said object-oriented programming uses self-contained objects holding both methods and the data being processed.
parts.src: the 2024 Q5(a) mark scheme

try.stem: Fill the two gaps with words from the bank. The sentence is from the 2024 paper.

surface.text: Object-oriented programming uses self-contained {1} which contain both methods and the {2} being processed.

screens.title: Classes and objects: one plan, many objects
screens.goal: Tell a class from an object and explain how objects are made from a class.

say: Alex was one object. A game usually needs several characters that work the same way.
A [[class|1]] is the plan that says what data and methods every character will have.
An object is one actual character made from that plan, with its own values.
Making an object from a class is called creating an instance of the class.

anim.title: One biscuit cutter, many biscuits
anim.lead: Press Next to make biscuits from one cutter. Then see the same idea with the game characters.
steps: Here is a biscuit cutter. It is a shape for making biscuits. It is not a biscuit.
Press it once: the first biscuit. It has the cutter's shape.
Press it again: a second biscuit, the same shape.
Decorate them differently. Same shape from the same cutter, different icing on each.
The cutter is the class. Each biscuit is an object, also called an instance of the class.
Back to the game. A Character class, and two character objects made from it. Both have a position and a Move method. Each stores its own position value.
Where the picture stops being true: a cutter gives a shape only. A class also gives every object its methods, such as Move.

anim.title: The Character class in C#, one part at a time
anim.lead: This is the code behind the pictures. Press Next to reveal it a part at a time.
steps: Lines 1 to 8 define the class Character: the plan. Nothing has been made yet.
Line 3 says every Character stores a Position. Lines 4 to 7 give every Character a Move method that adds 1 to Position.
Line 9 creates the first object, named alex, with new Character(). Line 10 creates a second object, bea. Both start with Position 0.
Lines 11 and 12 store different values. alex's Position is 1 and bea's is 3. Each object keeps its own value.
Line 13 runs Move on alex only. alex's Position becomes 2. bea's Position stays 3.

parts.head: Class: the textbook definition
parts.say: A template or blueprint for an object. It defines the properties and methods for a group of objects.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19) and the class presentation. The specification does not define it.
points: template or blueprint: the cutter, or lines 1 to 8 of the code
defines the properties and methods: Position and Move
a group of objects: every character made from the class

parts.head: Object and instance
parts.say: An object is one item made from a class, with its own values. Making it is called instantiation, and the object is an instance of the class.

parts.head: What the examiner has credited
points: The 2025 Q7 mark scheme lists objects and classes among the object-oriented features worth describing.
parts.src: the 2025 Q7 mark scheme

parts.head: Say it in your own words
parts.say: A class is the plan. An object is one thing made from the plan. Two objects from one class have the same kinds of data and methods but their own values.

try.stem: True or false? Decide for each statement.

rows: The biscuit cutter stands for a class.
Each biscuit stands for an object made from the class.
If alex's Position changes, bea's Position changes automatically too.
alex and bea both have a Move method because both were made from Character.

try.why: Each object stores its own values, so changing alex's Position leaves bea's alone. Both have Move because the class defines it for every object.

screens.title: Properties and methods: what an object has and what it can do
screens.goal: Name the properties and methods of an object.

say: A [[property|1]] is a named characteristic of an object that holds a value.
A method is something the object can do. It is a named block of instructions kept inside the object.
For Alex, Position is a property and Move is a method. Here is a second example.

picture.title: A dog object, with one method being called
lines: Properties: Name = Rex, Breed = Collie, Age = 3. Each one has a current value.
Methods: Sit, Bark, Fetch. Each one is a named block of instructions the dog object can run.
Another part of the program asks rex.Sit(). The Sit method runs and the dog sits.
breaks: A real dog decides for itself. A dog object does only what its methods say, and only when they are called.

parts.head: Properties: the textbook definition
parts.say: Contain code that facilitates reading and writing to the data within an object.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19). The specification does not define it.
points: In plain words: a property is how the program reads or changes one piece of an object's data, such as the dog's Age.

parts.head: Methods: the textbook definition
parts.say: The behaviours that an object can perform.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19). The specification does not define it.
points: In plain words: a method is a named block of instructions inside the object, such as Sit.

parts.head: What the examiner has credited
points: The 2025 Q7 mark scheme lists properties and methods among the object-oriented features worth describing.
parts.src: the 2025 Q7 mark scheme

Sit
Breed = Collie
Bark

screens.title: Inheritance: a new class built from an existing one
screens.goal: Explain inheritance and say what the child class reuses and what it adds.

say: Sometimes a new class is mostly the same as a class you already have.
[[Inheritance|1]] lets a child class reuse the data and methods defined in a parent class.
You then write only what is different in the child class.
That saves writing and testing the same code twice. It is one form of code reuse.

anim.title: From Animal to Dog
anim.lead: Press Next to build a Dog class from an Animal class.
steps: Start with a parent class called Animal. It has a Name characteristic and a Move method.
You need a Dog class. A dog is an animal, so it needs Name and Move too.
Dog inherits from Animal. Name and Move are reused in Dog without being written again.
Dogs also bark. Add a Bark method to Dog only. Animal does not get Bark.
Reused: Name and Move. Added: Bark. In this simple example only the difference was written.
Words: Animal is the parent class and Dog is the child class. The parent is also called the base class or superclass. The child is also called the derived class or subclass.

parts.head: Inheritance: the textbook definition
parts.say: Enables the properties of one class to be copied to another so that only the differences between the classes need to be reprogrammed.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19) and the class presentation. The specification does not define it.
points: Say: the child class reuses what the parent class defines and adds or changes only what is different.
Avoid absolutes such as the child copies everything or the child can change nothing. Real languages are more flexible than this introduction needs.

parts.head: Other names you will see
parts.say: Parent class, base class and superclass mean the same thing. Child class, derived class and subclass mean the same thing.

parts.head: What the examiner has credited
points: The 2025 Q7 mark scheme lists inheritance as an object-oriented feature and notes that both paradigms allow some code reusability.
parts.src: the 2025 Q7 mark scheme

try.stem: Dog inherits from Animal. For each member of Dog, was it reused from Animal or added in Dog?

rows: Name
Move
Bark

try.why: Animal defined Name and Move, so Dog reuses them. Bark was written in Dog because only dogs bark.

screens.title: Encapsulation and reuse: protecting an object's data
screens.goal: Explain encapsulation and give reasons object-oriented code is reused.

say: An object's data should not be changed by any code from anywhere in the program.
[[Encapsulation|1]] keeps an object's data inside the object. Other code reaches it only through the object's methods.
A method can check a request before it changes the data.

anim.title: The vending machine object
anim.lead: Press Next to ask the machine for a drink. Watch what happens to its stored data.
steps: A vending machine object holds five drinks. Its stored data: stock = 5.
Another part of the program wants a drink. It cannot reach in and change stock itself. It calls the machine's Dispense method.
Dispense checks the data first: is stock more than 0? Yes, it is 5.
Dispense releases one drink.
Dispense updates the data: stock = 4. Only the machine's own method changed it.
That is encapsulation. The data is protected inside the object and reached only through the methods the object provides.

parts.head: Encapsulation: the textbook definition
parts.say: Hides an object's data so that it can only be directly accessed by the methods within the object.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19) and the class presentation. The specification does not define it.
points: Ideas that earn credit: data hiding or information hiding, protecting data from being changed by mistake, and access only through the object's methods.
Do not claim that all data is automatically private. The programmer decides what is hidden.

parts.head: Why object-oriented code is reused
parts.say: Objects can be programmed and maintained independently. Objects can be reused in different programs by different developers. The internal implementation is hidden, so an object can be used without knowing how it works inside.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19)
points: The 2025 Q7 mark scheme credits encapsulation or information hiding, and notes that both paradigms allow some code reusability.

try.stem: Inheritance or encapsulation? Decide for each statement.

rows: Dog reuses Name and Move from Animal and adds Bark.
The vending machine's stock can only be changed through its Dispense method.
A child class is built from a parent class.
An object's data is hidden and reached through its methods.

try.why: Inheritance is about one class reusing another. Encapsulation is about protecting an object's data behind its methods.

screens.title: Compare procedural and object-oriented programming
screens.goal: Describe both paradigms and compare them, as the six-mark question asks.

say: The exam can ask you to describe both approaches and compare them.
Describe means: say what each one is and name its features.
Compare means: say how they differ or what they share.

left.title: Procedural programming
rows: Organised around procedures, also called functions or subroutines.
Planned top-down: the whole task, then smaller jobs, then steps.
Step-by-step instructions run in sequence inside each procedure.
Data is passed to a procedure when it is called, like 4 and 7 to CalculateSum.
Example languages: C, COBOL, FORTRAN.

right.title: Object-oriented programming
rows: Organised around objects that keep data and methods together.
Classes are the plans. Objects are made from them.
Properties hold an object's data. Methods are what it can do.
Inheritance lets a child class reuse a parent class.
Encapsulation protects an object's data behind its methods.
Example languages: C#, Java, Python.

parts.head: The multiple-choice version
parts.say: Object-oriented programming uses classes and inheritance whereas procedural programming uses procedures and top-down design.
parts.src: the 2021 Q1(b) mark scheme, the correct option

parts.head: The six-mark version
parts.say: 2025 Q7 was marked in levels. Level 3, 5 to 6 marks: both approaches fully described, at least three features, some comparison, and a good standard of spelling, punctuation and grammar.
parts.src: the 2025 Q7 mark scheme
points: Features the scheme lists. Procedural: procedures, functions or subroutines, step-by-step instructions, top-down design, functions to solve problems, an example language. Object-oriented: objects, classes, properties and methods, inheritance, encapsulation or information hiding. Both allow some code reuse.

parts.head: An example answer, annotated
sample: Procedural programming organises a program into procedures, each a named block of code that carries out one task.
It is planned top-down, and the instructions in each procedure run step by step, for example in C.
Object-oriented programming organises a program into objects made from classes. Objects hold data in properties and have methods.
Inheritance lets a child class reuse a parent class, and encapsulation protects an object's data behind its methods.
Both approaches allow code to be reused, but object-oriented programs keep data and methods together whereas procedural programs pass data to procedures.
points: No sentence earns a fixed mark on its own. The examiner reads the whole answer and places it in a level.

parts.head: Writing it
points: Clear sentences. Accurate terms. An explanation that stays on the question.

blocks.watch: Quality of written communication counts in the six-mark question: full sentences and correct terms.

try.stem: Which statement correctly compares the two paradigms?

opts: Object-oriented programming uses objects and methods whereas procedural programming uses classes and top-down design.
Object-oriented programming uses classes and methods whereas procedural programming uses procedures and objects.
Object-oriented programming uses classes and objects whereas procedural programming uses methods and inheritance.
Object-oriented programming uses classes and inheritance whereas procedural programming uses procedures and top-down design.

try.why: Classes and inheritance belong to object-oriented programming. Procedures and top-down design belong to procedural programming.

screens.title: Software development environments
screens.goal: Explain what a software development environment is and name its editing features.

blocks.bridge: So far: how programs are organised. Now: the tools programmers use to write them.

say: A [[software development environment|1]] is the program you write programs in. Visual Studio is one.
It brings the tools for writing, running and testing code together in one place.
Its editor has features that make writing code faster and less error-prone. Here are seven of them.

anim.title: Seven editing features, one at a time
anim.lead: A small C# program in a Visual Studio-style editor. Press Next to see one feature working.
steps: Here is a small C# program in a Visual Studio-style editor. Press Next to see one editing feature at a time.
Line numbering. Every line has a number, so an error message can say exactly where to look.
Colour-coded text. Keywords, strings and comments are shown in different colours, so the code is easier to read.
Collapsible code sections. A block can be folded away, so a long program is easier to move around.

Code completion, also called auto completion. Type Con and the editor offers Console. Pick it instead of typing the whole word. Code completion and auto completion are two names for ONE feature. In an exam, list it once.

Syntax-error assistance. A missing semicolon is underlined in red with a message, before you run anything. The mark schemes put this on the same line as IntelliSense. IntelliSense and syntax-error assistance count as one mark.
Automatic indentation, also called auto indent. Press Enter inside a block and the next line is indented for you.
Clipboard. Copy a line and paste it somewhere else, in this file or another.
That is seven different features. In an exam, name different ones. Code completion and auto completion are the same feature. IntelliSense and syntax-error assistance earn one mark between them.

screens.title: Code translation and compilers
screens.goal: Explain why code is translated and what a compiler does.

say: You write [[source code|1]] in a high-level language such as C#. People can read it.
The processor runs only machine code: binary instructions.
So the source code must be translated into machine code before the computer can run it.
A compiler translates the whole program before it runs. An interpreter translates and runs it one statement at a time.

anim.title: From source code to machine code
anim.lead: Press Next to follow two lines of C# through translation.
steps: Source code: two lines of C#, written by the programmer in a high-level language.
Translation: the compiler reads the source code and translates it.
Machine code: binary instructions the processor can carry out. The 1s and 0s shown here are illustrative, not the real output.
Why translate at all: the computer cannot carry out source code directly. It understands only machine code.

anim.title: Compiler and interpreter, side by side
anim.lead: The same three-line program goes through both. Press Next.
steps: Two kinds of translator. Left: a compiler. Right: an interpreter. The same program is on both sides.
Compiler: it translates the whole program first, before anything runs.
Compiler: the machine code is saved in a separate file from the source code. That file can be run again later.
Interpreter: it takes the first statement, translates it and runs it.
Interpreter: then the next statement, and the next, while the program is running. No separate machine-code file is kept.
Errors: a compiler reports the syntax errors after attempting to compile the whole program. They must be fixed before the program will run. An interpreter stops when it reaches the faulty statement.

anim.title: What a compiler does
anim.lead: Each task with a tiny example. The mark schemes credit these as a list in any order.
steps: A compiler does several tasks on the source code. Here they are one at a time, each with a tiny example.
Lexical analysis: split the source code into tokens. The statement int total = 4 and its closing semicolon become five tokens.
Syntax analysis: check that each statement follows the language's grammar. int total = 4 has no semicolon, so a syntax error is reported.
Semantic analysis: check the meaning. total was declared as an int, so storing "hello" in it is a type mismatch. A name that was never declared is reported too.
Include library code: Console.WriteLine is not written in your file. The compiler brings in the library code that provides it.
Generate machine code: the checked program is translated into machine code and saved, ready to run.

parts.head: Why code is translated
parts.say: Program code must be translated into machine code so that the computer can understand and execute the instructions.
parts.src: the textbook (chapter 19) and the class presentation
points: 2019 Q1(e)(i) and 2021 Q2(b)(i) credited: turned into machine code, 0s and 1s or binary. So the computer can understand it. So it can be executed. To change it to object code.

parts.head: What a compiler does
points: Processes each statement in the source code
Checks syntax, called syntax analysis, and reports errors
Lexical analysis
Semantic analysis
Includes library code, called pre-processing
Translates the program into machine code: machine code is generated
parts.src: the 2019 Q1(e)(ii) and 2021 Q2(b)(ii) mark schemes, which accept these in any order

parts.head: Compiler versus interpreter
points: A compiler translates the whole program before it is executed and stores the machine code in a separate file from the source code.
A compiler reports the syntax errors it found after attempting to compile the program.
An interpreter translates and executes the program as it runs, one statement at a time.
parts.src: the 2024 Q5(b) mark scheme

blocks.watch: A common mix-up: which translator deals with the whole program first? The compiler translates the whole program before it runs. The interpreter translates as it runs, one statement at a time.

try.stem: True or false? These four statements are from the 2024 paper.

rows: Translators can be either compilers or interpreters
Interpreters translate the whole program at once whilst compilers translate the program line by line
A compiler reports all syntax errors after attempting to compile the program
After a program has been compiled the machine code version of the program is stored in a separate file from the source code

try.why: It is the compiler that translates the whole program at once. An interpreter works one statement at a time.
